title: RAG, Part 2: Chunking, Vector Databases and Reranking

scenes.text: In episode 7, we learned that RAG lets AI look things up before answering. [1] But how does it find the right paragraph, among thousands of pages? [2] Let's open the engine room of RAG. Part 2.

Here's the full RAG pipeline. [1] First, split your documents into small chunks. [2] Turn each chunk into an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning. [3] Store them in a vector database. [4] When a question comes in, find the closest chunks, [5] then rerank them, and send the best few to the AI.

Let's start with chunking. [1] If chunks are too big, the useful sentence gets buried in noise. [2] If chunks are too small, they lose context, like half a sentence. [3] A common choice is a few hundred words per chunk, with a little overlap, so ideas aren't cut in half.

Next, embeddings, from episode 6. [1] Each chunk becomes a point on a map of meaning. [2] Chunks about refunds cluster together, and so do chunks about shipping. [3] A question like, can I get my money back, lands near the refund chunks, even without the word refund.

data.heading: Chunks on a meaning map
query: Can I get my money back?
data.note: Found by meaning, not exact words

scenes.text: A vector database stores millions of these points, [1] and finds the nearest ones to your question in milliseconds. [2] It returns the top K matches, say the top 20. [3] Popular ones include Pinecone, Chroma, and pgvector.

data.definition: A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones closest in meaning to a query.

scenes.text: Now, reranking. [1] Vector search is fast, but a bit rough. It finds chunks that sound similar. [2] A reranker is slower, but smarter. It reads the question and each chunk together, and scores how well it actually answers. [3] So we search wide, then rerank, and keep the best few.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think, with a giant context window, you can skip retrieval and just paste everything. [2] Long prompts cost more, run slower, and the AI can miss details buried in the middle. Good retrieval still wins.

data.myth: With a giant context window, just paste everything and skip retrieval.
data.fact: Huge prompts cost more, run slower, and details in the middle get missed. Good retrieval still wins.
data.tip: Send the best, not the most

scenes.text: Quick quiz! What does a reranker do? [1] Pause and think, and if you get it right, comment below! <pause 3.2> [2] It re-scores the retrieved chunks by how well they actually answer the question!

data.question: A reranker…
options: Re-scores retrieved chunks by how well they answer

scenes.text: Let's recap. [1] Chunk documents into right-sized pieces, with overlap. [2] Embed each chunk as meaning numbers. [3] A vector database finds the closest chunks fast. [4] And a reranker picks the best few for the AI. [5] Next, RAG part three, hybrid search, and measuring quality. Follow AI Maastaaru!
